subject: hubble space telescope
title: What If You Pointed a Telescope at Nothing for 10 Days? Hubble Did in 1995

scenes.text: What if you aimed the best telescope ever built at nothing, for ten days? In 1995, someone did.
Director Robert Williams picked a blank patch near the Big Dipper, the size of a tennis ball seen from 100 meters. Some senior astronomers called it a waste of Hubble's time.
December 18 to 28, 1995. 342 exposures, more than 100 hours, catching light four billion times fainter than your eye can see.
The empty patch held about 3,000 galaxies. Some of their light had been travelling for 12 billion years.
Hubble stared again in 2004, for a million seconds: 10,000 galaxies. By 2012, 23 days of exposure showed light from 13.2 billion years ago.
Ten days spent on nothing. It turned out there is no such thing as empty sky.

description:
What if you pointed the Hubble Space Telescope at an apparently empty patch of sky and kept staring for ten days? In December 1995, director Robert Williams used his own discretionary time to do exactly that, despite misgivings from some senior astronomers.
342 exposures over 10 consecutive days of a patch just 2.6 arcminutes wide revealed about 3,000 galaxies, some at distances of around 12 billion light-years. Later deep fields went further: the 2004 Ultra Deep Field found about 10,000 galaxies, and the 2012 eXtreme Deep Field, with 23 days of total exposure, reached light from 13.2 billion years ago.
What should we run through next?

first_comment: That first patch covers about one 24-millionth of the sky. If you could stare at any spot in the universe for ten days, where would you point?
